title: Carry-Forward explained: what it costs to storm the Throne
description: BumpOne.lol active value is credit, not a debt you repay. Worked example with real numbers from the board mechanics.
body:
# Carry-Forward, explained: what it costs to storm the Throne

The stake you put on the board is capital that follows you.

## The mechanic

On BumpOne.lol, every profile has **active value** - the dollars you've
staked, still standing. Rank is active value, sorted descending. #1 has
more than #2, always.

When you want to move up, you don't buy a new position. You pay the
difference between what you hold and what your target holds, plus a $10
minimum top-up. The money you've already put in keeps working for you.

## The worked example (numbers are the rulebook, not marketing)

Say the board looks like this:

- #1 holds $700
- #50 is you, holding $500

You want the Throne (the colossal center tile that marks #1 on the board).
What do you pay?

**$700 − $500 + $10 = $210.**

Your active value becomes $500 + $210 = $710. That's not $710 paid for the
Throne - $500 of it is the stake you already had. You just topped up
$210 to be strictly above the King, because a takeover must *exceed* the
target - there are no ties, no photo finishes, no permanent rank ceiling.

Now every profile below you computes the same equation about *you*.
And the displaced King gets the notification.

## Why the design matters

Two properties fall out of this, straight from the product rules:

1. **Climbing is cumulative.** Nobody wipes your progress. Fall to the
   Graveyard (the analog billboard below the visible 100), come back, and
   your next top-up still builds on what you've spent before - the market
   keeps the score.
2. **The gap is always a number.** To take a position, you can see exactly
   what it costs, because spends are public. Profiles show both active
   value and lifetime spend. There is no hidden buy-in, no mystery pricing.

That second rule is the honest part of an attention market. A competitor
can't be secretly richer than they look. Their spend is on the profile,
right next to their current strength.

## The smallest legal move: $10

Entry is $10 minimum. That won't take a Throne - but it takes a tile of
your own on the outer ring, and the ranking doesn't stop at 100.

---

Do the math on whoever is at the top of your category. The number you
land on is probably smaller than you think.

[Run the math →](https://bumpone.lol)

title: The Internet Attention Market That Never Sleeps
description: Paid boards are static tables. BumpOne.lol is a live arena where attention is traded between real players in real time - here is how the board actually works.
body:
# The Internet Attention Market That Never Sleeps

There is a wall. It holds one hundred tiles, arranged like a colosseum. In
the center sits a throne - the biggest tile on the board. Right now,
somebody owns it.

You can take it from them tonight.

## A market, not a list

Every "paid leaderboard" on the internet works the same way: buy a row,
sit still, decay slowly. Nobody competes because nobody can. A rank number
is just a receipt.

BumpOne.lol treats attention the way a market treats anything worth having:
as a contested asset. Profiles buy **active value** with real dollars, and
active value is rank. The board is sorted by it, top to bottom, and it
moves all the time, because the people below you can outbid the people
above you - including you.

That changes what a purchase means. You are not renting a slot. You own a
position on a live board, and every position has a target on it.

## The board has geography

The top 100 isn't a flat table. It's structured like real estate:

- **The King Throne** - a single colossal tile at #1. Center of the board.
- **The Champions** - four anchor tiles on the cardinal points, #2 to #5.
- **The Elite Council** - #6 to #15, the inner ring.
- **The Vanguard** - #16 to #40, enhanced mid-tier tiles.
- **The Contenders** - #41 to #100 on the outer perimeter.

And below the visible hundred? The **Graveyard** - a billboard archive of
every profile that got knocked off the board. Nothing there is deleted.
Fall off, and you can walk back in and reclaim your turf whenever you're
ready.

When a takeover happens, it isn't quiet. It's a bump battle - a broadcast
event that shows who stormed the throne, who got displaced, and by how
much. The displaced get notified. They know exactly which door to knock on.

## Three ways to watch the fight

Attention is legible here, three different ways:

1. **Power** - the authoritative ranking, straight by dollars paid.
2. **Popular** - community-ranked, by emoji reactions.
3. **Trending** - momentum, by climb velocity and recent bump activity.

And transparency is the house rule: every profile shows its **active
value** (your current ranking strength) *and* its **lifetime spend**.
The board doesn't hide the economics. The economics are the story.

## Your stake carries forward

Here's the part that surprises people: you don't repay your full value
every time you climb. Your active value is credit. If you sit at #50 with
$500, and #1 holds $700, you don't pay $700 - you pay the difference plus
the $10 minimum. Your $500 rides with you into first place.

That's what makes it a market instead of an auction. You can challenge the
throne without deep pockets. You just need a bigger claim than the person
who's standing there.

---

The board is live right now. Somebody owns that throne, and somebody,
somewhere, is doing the math on taking it.

[Claim your turf →](https://bumpone.lol)

title: Three signals: how Power, Popular and Trending sort the board
description: One board, three simultaneous rankings - by dollars, by reaction, by momentum. Why BumpOne.lol makes the competition legible.
body:
# Three signals: how Power, Popular and Trending sort the board

A board that sorts one way sorts nobody. BumpOne.lol runs **three
discovery signals at once** on the same arena, because attention isn't one
dimension - and the design never pretends it is.

## Power - the market's spine

Power is the authoritative ranking: straight by active value, dollars
staked, descending. This is the board's ground truth. #1 in Power owns the
King Throne - the massive center tile that every takeover drama resolves
around. If you want the game's scoreboard, this is it. Dollars on the
table, sorted, visible.

## Popular - the crowd's own vote

Popular re-ranks profiles by emoji reactions. A profile the crowd loves
can ride far above profiles with bigger budgets on this signal - and that
shows up honestly as a separate ranking, not as a "score" blended into
everything else. Money sorts one list; affection sorts another; both are
forwarded to everyone looking at the wall.

## Trending - who's moving right now

Trending is momentum - climb velocity and recent bump activity. The profile
that is #60 today and #18 by the weekend: trending is how that run
gets spotted, early, while it's still a run. Fast risers surface on a
dedicated ranking of their own instead of being invisible between the
static tiers.

## Why three lists beat one score

Because each signal answers a different question a visitor might actually
be asking:

- "Who's the strongest?" → Power
- "Who does the crowd actually like?" → Popular
- "Who's worth watching this week?" → Trending

The mechanics stay market-honest throughout. Spends are public on every
profile (active value today, lifetime spend across the account), so none
of these rankings can be gamed into looking richer or bigger than the
board's own data says. It's a paid attention market that shows its own
ledger - power from real money, popularity from real people, momentum
from real movement.

---

Watch all three for a week and you'll notice the board has protagonists.

[Pick your signal →](https://bumpone.lol)
